english.html: when she is violated and carried off from one place to another by force <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>, but also when she is seduced and suborned by ruses, cunning, baits and false persuasions <sup class="mk" data-key="c">c</sup>; and then the Rape is punished no less than if it had been committed and executed by force <sup class="mk" data-key="d">d</sup>: both because a will extorted by wiles, or by some fraud, does not warrant the trickster, nor cover his crime <sup class="mk" data-key="e">e</sup>; and also because to persuade craftily, with ruses and false and honeyed enticements, is no less than to force and constrain <sup class="mk" data-key="f">f</sup>. And so, in like terms, Ulpian the Jurisconsult answers that he who keeps a free person in his house, although it be with that person's consent, and he is content with it, if nevertheless such affection and contentment proceed from the cunning, subornation and false representations of him who keeps him, is no less culpable than if he kept him by force <sup class="mk" data-key="g">g</sup>. And thus are to be understood the texts of our laws which seem to require, for the crime of Rape, force and violence <sup class="mk" data-key="h">h</sup>. From this there follows a kind of excuse for the said de Rols: for a woman who has been forced cannot be charged with adultery, nor with any lechery <sup class="mk" data-key="i">i</sup>, even though for shame she has not at once declared it, and has expressly forbidden that it be told to her husband <sup class="mk" data-key="k">k</sup>; nay, the Emperor in these cases wills that the reputation of a woman of worth be inviolably and perpetually preserved to her <sup class="mk" data-key="l">l</sup>.

Lex [illa], at the end, and c. De raptoribus (canon numbers unverified)

notes.gloss: Causa 36 of the Decretum is the causa on raptus.

notes.citation: Code 9.13.1 (as at {a}); Authenticum, coll. 9, the Novel De raptu mulierum (Nov. 143 = Nov. 150, Ut raptae mulieres non nubant raptoribus), § 1; the Gloss on the rule Scienti in the Liber Sextus, De regulis iuris (VI, de reg. iur., reg. 27, Scienti et consentienti non fit iniuria neque dolus)
notes.original: l. vn. C. de rap. vir. P. j. de ra. mul. col. ix. Gloſe au c. ſcienti. de reg. iur. au vj.
notes.gloss: The rule says no wrong is done to one who knows and consents; the gloss is cited for its limit — consent procured by fraud is no consent.

notes.citation: Digest 47.10 (De iniuriis et famosis libellis), l. 1, § Usque adeo (D. 47.10.1.5, Ulpian); Code 1.7 (De apostatis), l. Eum (fragment not identified)
notes.original: l. P. vſque adeo. D. de in iur. l. eum. C. de apoſta.
notes.gloss: D. 47.10.1.5: the wrong done to our children touches our own honour, so that even if a son is sold with his consent the father has the action for iniuria in his own name — the wrong to the husband or father subsists though the woman was willing. The print's l. P. has lost the law's number (l. j.); the same text was cited at annot-046 {f} under a title there printed de in ius.

notes.citation: Code 9.13.1 (as at {a}), and Baldus (Balde) on it

l. j. P. perſuadere. D. de ſer. corrup.
notes.gloss: Persuadere autem est plus quam compellere atque cogere sibi parere — to persuade is more than to compel and force to obey; Coras's "no less than to force and constrain".

notes.citation: Digest 43.29 (De homine libero exhibendo), l. 3, § Si quis volentem (cf. D. 43.29.3.5, Ulpian; paragraph number unverified)
notes.original: l iij P. ſi. qs volentem. D. de lib. ho. exhib.
notes.gloss: The interdict against one who keeps a free man with evil intent: a willing person is not held with dolus — unless the willingness was procured by fraud. The margin's qs is the abbreviation of quis.

notes.citation: Institutes 4.18, § Item lex Iulia, and Decretum C. 36 q. 1, c. Lex and c. De raptoribus — the same places as at {b}

notes.citation: Digest 48.5 (Ad legem Iuliam de adulteriis coercendis), l. Si uxor, § Si quis plane (D. 48.5.14(13), Ulpian; paragraph unverified), and l. Vim passam (D. 48.5.40(39) pr., Papinian); Digest 3.1 (De postulando), l. 1, and its § Removet (D. 3.1.1.6, Ulpian)
notes.original: l. ſi vxor. P. ſi quis plane. l. vim paſſã. D. de adult. l. j. l remouet. D. de poſtul
notes.gloss: Papinian: a woman who has suffered violence has not offended against the lex Iulia de adulteriis. D. 3.1.1.6: one who has been violated by brigands or enemies is not to be marked with infamy (non debet notari). Coras cites Removet as a separate law; it is a paragraph of l. 1.

notes.citation: Digest 48.5.40(39) pr., l. Vim passam, cited above at {i}
Code 9.9 (Ad legem Iuliam de adulteriis et de stupro), l. Foedissimam (C. 9.9.20, Diocletian and Maximian)
notes.gloss: The constitution distinguishes the most foul wickedness of women who prostitute themselves from the case of those taken by force, whose reputation is to suffer no injury — Coras's "the Emperor wills that the reputation of a woman of worth be preserved to her". The same law is cited at annot-082 {u}. The transcribers could not settle whether the print's double s is ſs or ſſ; the word is the same.

notes.citation: Digest 48.13 (Ad legem Iuliam peculatus et de sacrilegis et de residuis), ll. 1, 4, 6 and 9 (the vulgate numbering of the title differs from the modern); Decretum, C. 17 q. 4, c. Si quis contumax and c. Quisquis (canon numbers unverified)
notes.original: l. i. l. iiij. l. vj. l. ix. D. ad l. Iul. peculat. c. ſi quis contumax c. quiſ quis. xvij. q. iiij.
notes.gloss: D. 48.13 is the Roman law of sacrilege as theft of sacred things; C. 17 q. 4 the Decretum's treatment of sacrilege and the violation of churches.
